asDecan.p: Your Sun is in the first ten degrees of Aquarius, and the Golden Dawn gave that slice to Venus. Venus has no special standing in Aquarius. It's a visitor, neither helped nor held back, so it takes its tone from whoever owns the sign, Saturn in the old system and Uranus in the modern one. Left to itself Venus will smooth things over to keep everyone happy. With Saturn leaning on it, it can't let something unfair go, even when letting it go would make the evening easier. These are also the opening degrees, fixed air at its freshest, so your views arrive early and stay put. Mercury's Six comes next and is about getting away to calmer water, and the Moon's Seven slips off quietly with what it wants. The first slice stays and argues. The Star is still your Sun card, and the Five is a closer look at one corner of it. In the picture one man is gathering up swords while the other two walk off.

You like people, lots of them, and you're usually the one who knows everyone at a party a little. Let the group chat turn into a debate about something you care about, whether the landlord's allowed to do that or whether a film was actually any good, and you'll be up until one sending careful, reasonable paragraphs. At a family lunch you're the one who corrects your uncle's facts, politely, and then can't work out why the mood went flat. When a friend cancels on you twice you don't say you're hurt. You say it's fine, and you mean it in principle. Somewhere in your head there's a running tally of who's been fair to whom in your friendship group, going back years, and you'd be mortified if anyone found out how detailed it is.

What people underestimate is how cleanly you can separate a person from their opinion. Venus here borrows some of Saturn's backbone, so you can tell a friend her business plan has a hole in it and still be at her birthday the following week, with neither of you holding it against the other. You can have a proper row about politics with your brother-in-law over the barbecue and then help him carry the esky back to the car, and mean both. Someone can shout you down in a meeting and you'll ask them to lunch the next day, partly because you want to hear the rest of their argument. Early Aquarius Suns tend to keep friends on every side of a fight, and they often end up as the one person both camps will still talk to.

Other people's feelings are where this decan trips. Your partner comes home upset about a colleague and within two minutes you're explaining the colleague's side, because it's only fair, and your partner goes quiet and goes off to have a shower. You may well have been right about the colleague. It didn't help. There's another habit too. When an argument turns personal, you often stop arguing altogether and just leave, sometimes the room and sometimes the friendship, and you tell yourself it was the grown-up thing to do. The friend who fell out with you over a wedding seating plan three years ago probably still doesn't know why you went cold. You're generous with strangers and with causes, and a good deal stingier with the four or five people who actually need you.

When something goes badly, a redundancy or a break-up or a friend saying something cruel, your first move is to work out who was in the right. You'll lay it out for anyone who asks, calmly and in order, and people may think you're coping brilliantly. A week later you're usually still arguing it, only now it's in your head at two in the morning and you're drafting a message you'll never send. You get cooler with everyone, even people who had nothing to do with it, and they feel the draught without knowing where it's coming from. The thing that helps is a friend who'll take your side without weighing it up first. Tell them it hurt, let them say the other person was awful, and don't correct them, even if they've got a detail wrong.

Arguing is a big part of how you fall for someone. The first proper conversation that runs past midnight, where they disagree with you and don't back down, tends to be the moment you know. Venus in a Saturn-ruled sign likes a bit of resistance. The part people miss is that you also need to lose sometimes, to someone you respect, and a partner who always gives in to keep the peace slowly bores you, even if you'd never say so. The trouble comes in the small fights, whose turn it was to ring the plumber, who forgot to book the anniversary dinner, which you can win on the facts every single time. Winning those gets lonely after a while. Most of the long relationships I've seen with this Sun are with someone who laughs when you start quoting the evidence, and gets you laughing too.

Work that runs on a principle suits you. Advocacy, policy, community organising, user research, editing, law, running a volunteer group, any job where you get to argue for the people who aren't in the room. You've also got a good eye, which is the Venus in you, so design with a social point to it tends to pull you in. The pattern to watch is the internal fight. There's a restructure or a new process and you can see exactly why it's wrong, so you write the email, and you're right, and it goes through your way. Then you notice nobody's asked you to lunch for a month. When you can see a decision's wrong, go and talk to the person who made it before you put anything in writing. It's slower, and they tend to remember that you came to them first.

Twenty is usually when this decan is at its most combative. You've got strong views on nearly everything, you'll happily argue with a lecturer or a manager in front of everyone, and you lose a few friends to it without much regret. By the mid-thirties a lot of people with this placement have won at least one fight that cost them more than they expected, a sibling they stopped speaking to or a workplace they had to leave, and they get choosier about the next one. The views are still there. They just stop needing everyone to agree. The fifties tend to bring a warmer version of the same person, still the one who says the awkward thing at the committee meeting, only with more humour, and the people who've stuck around are usually the ones who were always willing to argue back.

For a fortnight, every time you feel the urge to correct someone in a group, a date, a statistic, a bit of history they've got slightly wrong, let it go and put a tick in the notes on your phone instead. At the end of each day, look at the ticks and ask whether any of those corrections would have changed anything. Mostly the answer is no. Keep going anyway, because the useful part is seeing how often the urge comes, and who it tends to come with.
